before: Cyril: …a human of Judah, a beloved newly planted.’ So a virtue of a shepherd is not to let loose upon sheep some animal of another form, so that they fall under somehow foreign mountings, lest it bear something of another nature, and having bent away from the natural good birth present in it; and the caretaker of vineyards, if he should be sensible and have practiced farming most excellently, would never endure the dry of the seeds to grow under the vines themselves, lest, the moisture being spent for them unto the alien, they themselves fall short concerning what is their own. Come then already somehow from an image now unto the spiritual: let us not allow the rational flocks to be led unholily under the sowings of the otherwise-teaching—intelligible ones clearly, and the introductions as in word; for the fruit from dissimilar resolve is very ugly, and the words of those not of like faith would become providers of base conceptions for those who have received them; and we being vineyards, and lying in the order of orchards, it is somehow fitting to be crowned with single-formed fruit, and to decline the double-natured mode. For there is no word unto natural likeness for wheat and clusters. So let there be for none of us a place of alien seeds.
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: And in another way also he shows the differently mannered as unjoined and incompatible, and split from communion toward one another, having set beside as a type the most outlandish and altogether strange joining of the rational animal toward what is not such, but of another form and out of tribe. And indeed he also says in Exodus: ‘Whoever should sleep with a beast, you will kill him by death.’ (Isaiah 5:7) And more clearly again in Leviticus: ‘And whoever should give his lying in a four-footed animal, let him be put to death by death, and you will kill the four-footed; and a woman who should approach unto every beast to be forced by it, you will kill the woman and the beast; let them be put to death by death; they are liable.’ (Exodus 22:19) For converses and as it were intelligible mixings and joinings toward those for whom it would least be fitting, and for whom the mind has sickened unto unreason the last, are providers of death, both for those who corrupt and for those who endure the corruption as voluntary.
Palladius: Most uprightly and very holily the law speaks.

Cyril: And you would still marvel also at this; for there were somehow some who, as from unbearable grasping, even if they should not wish to endure the corruption from uprightness of thoughts unto what holds sideways, also somehow from necessity, perhaps not without tears, suffer the wandering. So the law did not think fit to overlook even such a race as without help.
Palladius: What sort of thing do you mean?
Cyril: The one bound tight with a yoke of slavery and held down by the authorities of those who have bought them (Leviticus 20:15–16).

For just as a soldier who has thrown away the shield and fled the war must not be honored with second sealings, but already be punished, and pay accounts of unmanliness; in the same manner, I think, those so insulting a reverend and admirable grace must not be honored with a second gift of the Spirit, the first having been set aside, but already it is fitting they lie under penalties. And us ourselves also warm and sharp pleasures often persuade to count the slavery under the devil as bearable, and for the sake of corruptible and more earthy desires to be bound down in the yokes of sin. Yet he was giving even then the flesh-eating, not unto one, nor unto ten perhaps, but unto thirty days, through which the extension of the anger upon them is signaled. And even now he allows those who have turned aside ungovernably into worldly pleasures both to share, if they should choose, the fleshly things, and unto times sometimes long. For thus some are said to be handed over into an unapproved mind, to do the things not fitting. Palladius: Terrible truly is the matter, friend.

Cyril: Yet someone sometimes of those finishing among us, not yet very much fixed, yet having practiced a plastered and bastard love unto Christ, and such as putting around himself as it were a fleece the seeming to be God-loving, will be a bitter and unholy beast, both a monkey and facing-both-ways, so as at home and by night—I mean the having-escaped-notice—to cling to the demons’ worships, and somehow to think reasonably that he himself also can run past God, and out-reason the mind of the unspeakable nature. Cyril: And casting a thin eye of mind into what has been written, you would very well wonder at the beauty of the image.

Palladius: And what then is this?
Cyril: For the one was firstborn from Jacob, yet the other sprang from the maidservant Zilpah.
Palladius: True.

Palladius: The word has been made for us most excellently and rightly. Yet tell that: for what reason does he command to take the tail, and not the head, or the middle parts?
Cyril: For thus, friend, it had to be accomplished; since taking the tail, and not middle or head, is useful for the mystery.
Palladius: In what way?

Cyril: For the head is as it were beginning of every living thing, and the tail is end. Come then, let the whole race of man be reckoned for us as still a living thing for the present. Christ therefore took hold of the tail—that is, of those in the last and final ones; for he has descended in the last times of the age. But just as even if Moses took hold of the tail, the reshaping ran up even as far as the head (for the serpent was completely transformed into a rod)—in this same way, even if Christ laid hold of the last ones, yet the remolding through grace extends through the whole race and arrives even as far as the head itself—that is, Adam. For it is written that for this Christ died and rose, that he might be lord of both dead and living. Therefore with the last ones the redemption of those in the beginnings is also accomplished together.
Palladius: The word is persuasive for us, and the narration is not off the mark.

Cyril: Most firm therefore toward faith in this matter, he was also making him with two other powers by divine signs. Palladius: You have spoken well.

Cyril: He said that the sacrifice for them must be offered with two calves, one full-grown and one a year old, that is, tender and young (Numbers 8:8). The full-grown one is for the whole burnt offering, and fine flour mixed with oil is burned together with it; the other, for sin, is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12), for that is how the sacrifices for sin are completed. And here again Christ is in both. In the calf for the whole burnt offering he is wholly holy and a sweet-smelling fragrance to God the Father on our behalf (Ephesians 5:2), bringing to the saints the delight and gladness of the life that is in hope; for the fine flour mixed with oil was offered up together with the calf, and it will surely, I think, follow those who have honored the life that is in Christ. He is also the young calf for sin, consumed by fire, for ‘by his wound we were healed’ (Isaiah 53:5), as the Scriptures say. Notice that the full-grown calf is burned whole, while the yearling is slaughtered for sin (Numbers 8:12), so that through the two you may understand at once the One: most fragrant in a spiritual sense, as in the perfection of virtues, and slaughtered, as in simplicity and innocence. For he says: ‘I, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19). The laying on of hands by the people of Israel would show that the priestly race is brought to God as an offering on behalf of all and from all together. For he says: ‘The sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the heads of the Levites’ (Numbers 8:10). The Levites laid their hands on the heads of the sacrificial victims, which were slaughtered on their behalf as a type of Christ (Numbers 8:12). They did this not to bless them in any way, far from it, but as though by the laying on of hands to point to the God who bears our sins (Isaiah 53:4) and is offered in sacrifice for us, so that he might nail to his own cross the record of debt that stood against us (Colossians 2:14). You will understand that the people’s ordination of the Levites was carried out in the same way. For when they laid their hands on them, it was as though they were setting them before God in their own place for the sacred service, as chosen men. Then, the laying on of hands was the practice. But now that things have passed over to what is incomparably better, the people vote for those who are called through Christ to the sacred service, joining heartily in the cry that they are worthy; and they do this in the churches, just as, of course, those of old performed the laying on of hands upon the Levites at the sacred and divine tabernacle (Numbers 8:9). It is plain, then, that if an ordination took place neither in church nor in the presence of the people, it would be contrary to the divine will and outside the sacred laws. Once the Levites have been consecrated, they handle everything that belongs to the sacred service (Numbers 8:15).

Cyril: Two therefore are the trumpets; for double in churches is the proclamation of the consolation: for one carries the believers off unto dogmatic rightness, and adulterates down the word of the twisted ones; such as was the of those forbidding to marry, and teaching unfittingly to abstain from foods which God created unto partaking for the faithful. And when the cloud went up from the tent, after these things the sons of Israel set out; and in the place where the cloud stood, there the sons of Israel were encamping; through the Lord’s command (John 17:24) the sons of Israel will encamp, and through the Lord’s command they will set out. All the days in which the cloud overshadows upon the tent, the sons of Israel will encamp; and whenever the cloud is drawn upon the tent more days, the sons of Israel will also keep God’s watch, and will not set out; and it will be whenever the cloud shelters days in number upon the tent, through the Lord’s voice they will encamp, and through the Lord’s command they will set out; and it will be whenever the cloud comes to be from evening until morning, and the cloud goes up in the morning, and they will set out by day or night, and the cloud goes up, they will set out by day, or a month’s days with the cloud’s overshadowing increasing upon it, the sons of Israel will encamp, and will not set out, because through the Lord’s command they will set out. For this also would show most clearly our Savior’s economy unto us. For those having come near him through the faith, and already having been shown intimates and brothers, through partaking of Holy Spirit, and having become sharers of a divine nature, he released from debts, they having paid out nothing; for he did not seek from them the justices of the transgression, although they were owing to him the accounts of the things lived by them; yet those still alien, and all but also other-raced, through their destructive unbelief, and having come to be as farthest from the intimacy unto him, he set liable to the debts, and as still having the sin unwashed, he reasonably worked them debtor both to the justice and to needing to be punished; and at any rate he was addressing those having believed: ‘If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you.’ Yet to those dishonoring the true and Gospel education: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.’ (John 8:31–32) Do you understand then that for those intimates according to faith he announces he will release unto freedom, yet for those still alien and foreign, having died in the stumbles, he said they will pay back to the judge the accounts of their own faults?

Cyril: A most plentiful path then carries us off unto this. And at any rate raising us unto the continual remembrance of the things having been legislated, the lawgiver says: ‘And you will cast these words into your heart and into your soul, and you will fasten them as a sign upon your hand, and they will be unshaken before your eyes, and you will teach them to your children, to speak them sitting in a way and lying down and rising, and you will write them upon the doorposts of your houses and of your gates, in order that you may be many-dayed, and days of your sons upon the earth which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, just as the days of the heaven upon the earth.’ (Deuteronomy 11:18) And what again is the ‘Fasten them upon your hands,’ (Numbers 15:37–41) he made clear in Numbers. before: guarding not to be without share for the word. For if, he says, an ox or donkey falls, the one having toiled will pay back. And he names ox and donkey again not simply, but as in a deep word; and he says ox, in order that you may understand the sacred and clean race; yet donkey, in order that you may put together the unsacred and unclean; for the unclean is not brought according to law unto a sacrifice for God; and we say a sacred and clean race are those already having been made holy through the faith; yet unsacred and unclean—those not yet having been cleansed through the holy baptism, but still having the pollution of the sin in-melted. Like then as if he should say, If some harm should become, either about some of those already baptized and sealed through the grace unto the intimacy as toward God, or then unto some perhaps of those not yet such, the provider of the scandal will owe a justice, and the having died will remain for him—that is, the death of the one having suffered will become his. At any rate the Savior himself also makes us safe saying: ‘Whoever should scandalize one of these little ones believing into me, it benefits him that a millstone of a donkey be hung around his neck, and he be sunk in the sea’s (Matthew 18:6) depth.’ Therefore one must cover the pit—that is, make the word about the mysteries safe with exactness, lest either a baptized one or one still outside be destroyed. And when teachers’ words as flames or fire fall upon the trickings of the other-doctrined and of Greeks, advocating for the dogmas of the truth, and go against thorn alone, and burn down as useless and wild matter the writings beside those, yet do not wrong together grain or ear—that is, let the mystagogues be sober, lest somehow they also damage something of the dogmas of the truth; or let him know, he says, who does not endure to do this with safety, that if somehow something of the necessary things unto benefit should become burned down together with the base things, he will pay back the accounts of the carelessness. Thorn then is the most foul and profane door-mouthing of the distorted ones; yet grain and ear is the soul-benefiting and most nourishing word of the truth (Matthew 18:6) (Matthew 13:24–30)

before: God and his law. And Moses’ father-in-law said to him: You are not doing this word rightly; you will not be able to do it alone. And now listen to me, and I will counsel you, and God will be with you. Become you to the people the things toward God, and you will bring up their words toward God, and you will testify to them the ordinances of God and his law, and you will signal to them the ways in which they will walk in them, and the works which they will do. And you look out for yourself from all the people powerful men, he says, and they will judge the people.’ And after other things again: ‘And Moses heard,’ (1 Kings 18:21) it says, ‘his father-in-law’s voice, and did as many things as he said to him.’
Palladius: Come then again to me, and taking each in part, clarify.

Cyril: Or do you not say the Midianite is foreign-born and from the nations? For he did not spring from Abraham’s root; and he was also otherwise a sacrificer and servant of the will-worship then customarily practiced upon the earth. For they were worshiping, as much account has it, and were thinking among themselves, to a most high God just as indeed also Melchizedek; yet they were also receiving perhaps other gods, numbering with him the exceptional of the creatures—earth and heaven, sun and moon, and the more notable of the stars; and an ancient fault is the corruption and wandering upon this, and it extends even until now and stretches on. For some of those in Phoenicia and Palestine still raving think thus, who name themselves god-fearing, yet walk a middle path of religion, cleaving purely neither to the Jews’ customs nor to the Greeks’, but as it were tossed and divided unto both. And when those from Israel once chose to think thus the prophet Elijah was rebuking saying: ‘Until when will you limp upon both the hams? either Baal, Baal, or to God, God.’ (Exodus 18:17–24) Jethro therefore was also, as is likely, administering some such manner of religion. Who when he knew the things come to be from God toward salvation of those from Israel, being charmed by august and admirable narrations, arrives with all house and all kin toward the holy Moses; who when he saw, received him gladly and has brought him into his own tent. And he narrates more precisely the achievements through the divine strength very well. And the wonder-works beyond every word. For the multitude of those wandering is called unto a change of mind as toward God—I mean the nations—first from hear-sayings which someone might make concerning God, then thus themselves through themselves as it were deserting toward the divine law—that is, the catechesis through holy letter. So that it also runs into the first tent. For the law is introductory; then, having been persuaded by the more ancient narrations, it moves over also unto choosing thereafter to think that God is one and alone, and indeed also unto the need to bear fruit to him. For the Midianite, having heard Moses’ narration, ‘Now I have known,’ he says, that the Lord is great beyond all the gods;

before: Palladius said: I would reasonably ask, then, what the delay of the sanctification according to faith was — why you say the sign is in the older place and the thing that surpasses it in the second.

Cyril: Did we not just say that it was the work of an admirable and unspeakable skill, that the Law which condemns should leap up in time before the faith that justifies? Or does not the light shine in the darkness? And is not power perfected in weakness, according to what is written?
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: So the Law came in besides, so that the trespass might increase. For where there is no Law, there is no transgression either. And how would anyone see the forgiveness of transgression and of the ease toward it, if the Law had not first condemned us? That what I say is true, and that the argument on this is not some faded or ugly thing, Paul will help, saying, 'So the Law was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom it has been promised, ordained through angels.' (Galatians 3:19) And being very wise, he tries to cut off in advance the inventions and questions that will sometimes be found by some. For it was likely that some would blame the delay of the righteousness in faith, and say that the coming-in of the Law in between became a setting-aside of that ancient promise. That is why he says, 'Is the Law then against the promises of God (Galatians 3:21)? Let it not be. For if a Law had been given that was able to make alive, righteousness would truly have been in Law. But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Before the faith came, we were guarded under Law, being shut up into the faith about to be revealed to us. So the Law became our tutor unto Christ, so that we might be justified from faith. But when the faith has come we are no longer under a tutor, for you are all sons of God through the faith in Christ Jesus.' (Galatians 3:25)

And he makes the question white-clear, as it were, by adding, 'This I say: a covenant previously ratified by God, the Law that came after four hundred and thirty years does not annul, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance is from Law, it is no longer from promise. But God has granted it to Abraham through a promise.' (Galatians 3:18) So the Law, having shut us up into sin, tutored us unto Christ, for the end of Law and prophets is Christ. That is why he also said to the peoples of the Jews who had not believed him, 'If you believed Moses, you would believe me. For he wrote about me.' (Romans 4:15) We are justified, then, not from works of Law, but rather by the faith in Christ. 'For as many as are from works of Law are under a curse. For it is written, Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them. But from the curse of the Law Christ bought all, having become' (Galatians 3:10) (Deuteronomy 27:26) (Galatians 3:13)

before: Cyril went on: 'And Abraham went up from Egypt, he and his wife, and all that was his, and Lot with him, into the wilderness. And Abraham was very rich, with cattle and silver and gold, and he went where he had gone out into the wilderness as far as Bethel, as far as the place where his tent was formerly, between Bethel and between Ai, to the place of the altar which he had made there at the beginning. And Abraham called there on the name of the Lord.' (Genesis 13:2–4) You understand, then, that with those who run up out of worldly incontinence into another holy life, all that is theirs must as it were set out together? For the forefather Abraham ran away from the Egyptians' land with his whole house and whole race, and I would add, with all his gear. For we must leave wholly, and love to shift as with a whole house into the wilderness, that is, into an undisturbed and clean condition of mind, from which also at the beginning man's nature went out, turning aside toward the worse by want of the goods from above. For the descent to strangers would mark this riddlingly, from a land as it were and tent of the things at the beginning and most dear, in which there is also an altar. For running back thus, until we come to be in the place and country of the altar at the beginning, that is, of the sanctification long grown with us, we too call on the God of all, saying that prophetic address: 'Lord, besides you we know no other. We name your name.' (Isaiah 26:13)
Palladius said: You have spoken most finely.

Cyril: And you may see the thing standing for us in no other way, if you also look well through the things that came to be upon the sons of Israel in their times; whom, when the Egyptians had taken them, a famine having pushed them down at the start, even those holy from above and from the root, and free, yoking them into a bondage unexpected and unpracticed for them, they forced wildly, having composed some such occasion of the cruelty upon them. 'For another king arose,' it says, 'over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. And he said to his race: Behold, the race of the sons of Israel, a great crowd, and it is strong beyond us; come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and, whenever war happens, these too will be added to the opponents, and having warred us out, they will go out from the land.' (Exodus 1:8–10) For it pained, I think, the ruler of the Egyptians' land, that those under a necessary bond, yoked not according to judgment, should even choose at some time to look toward freedom. 'And he set over them,' it says, 'taskmasters of the works, that they might maltreat them from the works, and they built fortified cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses, and On, which is Heliopolis.' (Exodus 1:11) For the fruits of the unbearable greed were the continual endurance of suffering upon clay and brickmaking, and cities towered with walls, and raisings of mounds in the fields, and these were accomplished unpaid and with long sweat for those who labored. For the world-rulers of this age, having taken under hand the wretched souls of men, wear them out in clay and brickmakings and in the things done toward earth and about earth, and having bound them to an evil and profitless trial (Ephesians 6:12).

before: Palladius: And what word would again be seen by us, of needing those condemned to be struck with blows by a number of forty alone? And how it shames some, say the thing beyond this.

Cyril: In many modes for us the mystery of Christ is well sketched through the ancient commandment, and the saving passion is somehow molded for us, in which and through which we have been released from everything able to harm, and casting us into incurable misfortunes; and as I said just now, the being released through seven years of those who have owed somehow hints the time of the release of all. For we have been justified in Christ, and have been taught to say in prayers, toward the Father and God in the heavens, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Deuteronomy 25:3); so also here, the advancing as far as forty blows for those striking, or being struck, the outrages through whips, shows the thrice-longed time for us of the economy with flesh of the Only-begotten, according to which by his bruise we were healed, and he himself has been softened because of our sins, those from Israel having insolently treated him, and Pilate having brought the blows upon the back, yet we have been taken out from penalty and punishment. For of old many were the whips of the sinner, according to what has been written, but Christ was whipped for us; for just as he died for all, so also again he was being whipped for all, being one worth all. And having cut the forty-day number into five times eight, you will find useful for the signifying of the time the five and the eight, for the Only-begotten has visited in a fifth time, according at least to the Gospel parable; for someone was hiring the workers into the vineyard; and going out about the first hour, and third and sixth, and ninth and eleventh; and he has been raised according to the eighth, having dissolved the power of death, and destroying together with it the mother of the brought-in corruption—that is, sin—which having been taken away, whips also must be idle, and the penalties and punishments through it. Therefore the law does not allow the whip still to overrun the fortieth number, as far as the presence of Christ and somehow standing the punishments, and marking down the time of the release. For the types of the truth travail the beauty. And one must know that Israel having struck against, was wandering the desert a fortieth year; for God swore with an oath not to lead them into the land of the promise. And this was a bound for them of the anger, and the time having passed, the anger has been loosed, and those from them crossed the Jordan, and entered into the land, the indignation not having overrun the fortieth year. So then a clear type also of this is some being struck as far as forty blows, for the time after this is of release, bringing in for us the mystical crossing of the Jordan, and indeed also flint knives—that is, the circumcision in spirit—and the generalship of Jesus (Isaiah 53:5) (Matthew 20:1–7) (Psalm 32:10) (Matthew 6:12)

The saints’ aim therefore, Palladius—even if they should contend above others’ life—is to love appropriating nothing of the things in the world; for thus they would be both wise and powerful, and filled with good hope, and very well walled by favors from above, and, know it well, friend, the matter is not otherwise. before: Cyril said: For it is always somehow slack and fallen back toward desire of the goods in hand, and it does not much long for the things of which it would have the power. Palladius said: True.

Cyril: It is needed, then, and wise, and of the things most profitable of all, to cut off well beforehand the wretched things and the assault of unwanted bondage, and to try to turn away swiftly from the things which, if we should come to a trial of them, we shall lie in every evil.

For choosing from the whole people Israel, and from every nation powerful men—I mean again the holy apostles and those called through faith, to whom it would be said well: ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people unto acquisition’ (1 Peter 2:9)—he arrayed with them against the ruler of this age; concerning whom the master of all, himself the one conquering all, says: ‘Now is judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast outside.’ (John 12:31) And the divine John also crowns with a bright vote those who have conquered with him and through him: ‘I write to you,’ (1 John 2:14) he says, ‘young men, that you are strong, and you have conquered the Evil One.’ (1 John 2:14) Or is what I say not true?
Palladius: Very much.

Cyril: And Moses said the arraying must be completed unto tomorrow; for Christ’s achievements did not appear in the time according to him; but they have rather been done in the next and neighboring—that is, after Moses and law. Then Moses goes up toward some hill and upon a crest of a mound, so that he might be able to look down upon the battle and Jesus’ achievements of all in it. For the mystagogy according to law also proportionately leads up toward being able as it were from afar to look upon Christ’s generalships. And when Moses was stretching up the hands, Israel was prevailing; and when letting them down, it was weak, and Amalek was prevailing; for unconquerable to the devil himself and to every enemy, and to the one wishing to ravage bitterly, has become not indeed all Israel, but as many as have honored the conformation toward Christ, through wearing his reproach—that is, the precious cross; for hands shown stretched out into air write clearly the schema of the cross. And as many as did not accept the cross have become easy to overrun for the enemies, not having the helper. When therefore Moses stretches out the hands for us, showing the schema of the cross, and Amalek falls having grown feeble, the schema signifies altogether for us those conquering Satan through the precious cross, and prevailing over the enemies. And when we see him letting the hands down, then Amalek prevailing, those who have come to be under the devil (Exodus 17:9–13)

Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: Therefore let the Yes, and the No, beside those having chosen to live best, be both need and power of an oath, and let it have been fixed rightly; for thus will also follow the needing to be believed. And blasphemy—what would I say hereafter, where it is, and that it may carry off unto evil those using it—which the ancient law also honors with bitter death. And Christ himself has also condemned it with inescapable and endless evils: ‘For whoever should say a word against the Son of the human, it will be forgiven him; yet whoever should say against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in the now age, nor in the coming.’ (Matthew 12:32) Calling Spirit the nature above body, which is God, to whom the one daring to send an unbridled tongue will reap the fruits of doorless-mouthing. ‘For lips of a fool lead him unto evils, according as it has been written. before: Cyril: Or will you not remember us having also said in the things already passed, that it is customary for the divine Scripture to liken the whole interval of the present and standing age to a week, because of the cycling-back unto the beginning of the days? For an end of a week is the Sabbath, and neighbor at once is the eighth, bringing in for us as somehow a new beginning of an age, through the resurrection of Christ.
Palladius: I will remember.

Cyril: He has visited then according to the Scriptures, upon a completion of the present age, and somehow as on a Sabbath—Christ—when he also released all, bound tight with cords of their own sins, and having owed him the accounts of the transgression. Therefore also in the Gospels he likens us to debtors saying: ‘Two debtors were to one human; the one owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. And not having to give back, he gifted both.’ (Luke 7:41–42) And still shaping for us the type of the prayer, ‘Thus then you pray,’ (Numbers 20:14–16) he says: ‘Our Father who is in the heavens, let your name be hallowed, let your kingdom come, let your will become as in heaven and upon the earth, give us today our bread for the coming day, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ (Matthew 6:9–12) So sideways then and riddlingly the law was hinting the divine mystery for us, commanding to make the release through seven years, and embarks us upon the paths of kindness, teaching to make better than money the loving unto brothers, persuading us to be ready to share and communal, and as somehow setting the gentleness unto brother and neighbor for now as a practice of the more ungrudging reverence unto all.
Palladius: Thus it holds. For I would agree with you wanting to speak most excellently.
Cyril: And the still greater, if you should learn, you would marvel, O Palladius.
Palladius: What sort?

For Pharaoh was fearing seeing the Hebrews stretching unto an unmeasured multitude; and attempting most wickedly to punish the rush and increase in this, ‘He set over them,’ it says, ‘overseers of the works, that they might maltreat them in the works.’ (Exodus 1:11–22) And the plan is overturned for them toward the opposite. For the maltreatment brought upon them was a pretext for them of the increase unto multitude, God managing the matter, and as it were setting his own grace against that one’s knaveries. For ‘Inasmuch as they were humbling them,’ (Habakkuk 1:16) it says, ‘by so much they were becoming more and were strong.’ (Psalm 124:1–4) For Satan brings on the afflictions, grinding his teeth against the saints, and always somehow selectively leaping upon those whom God was claiming as his own; for ‘His foods are choice,’ it says; but those toiling in these things will be better than them when tested; and the steadfastness in contests shows them altogether more famous, so that through things by which he would be thought to pain and to do evil, through these especially and not willingly he would benefit, and through what he has supposed he will take he finishes them stronger. And when the crafty sophism ends for Pharaoh unto an unexpected end, and through what he was maltreating he was also further benefiting, late and barely he perceives, and at once changes the manner of the plot; for having sent for the Hebrews’ midwives, ‘When you midwife the Hebrew women,’ he says, ‘and they are toward bearing, if it is male, kill it, and if female, preserve it.’ And the midwives feared God, and did not do just as the king of Egypt arranged for them, and they were keeping the males alive.’ And when his unholy and murderous counsel against the race is idle—for God was not letting the midwives act impiously—he thereafter goes over unto wronging openly, and no longer thought it right to pain secretly, but already somehow chooses war nakedly, and votes a harsh death of those being born. For ‘Pharaoh arranged,’ it says, ‘for all his people saying: Every male that is born to the Hebrews, throw into the river, and every female, keep it alive.’ For he cares for the female not at all—for woman is an unwarlike thing, and not elegant unto understanding; but the male pains him in both ways, as wise and most fight-ready. Therefore most sweet and altogether according to heart for the murderous dragon—I mean Satan—is a womanish mind of soul, made soft and without strength; and toward this also being sick with the unsuitedness unto wisdom, yet hated and abominated is the eagerness unto courage, and better than softness, and superior to cowardice, and the very most thoughtful. Because of this he keeps the female alive, and somehow stands off from the murderous counsel and plan upon it. For I think it is silly to seek to fight those already laid under from themselves, and sick from home with loving to be yoked under; but he stifles as it were the male, casting him into circumstances of trials. Cyril: I do not say that. For it was not oracled in vain. It was given rather 'for help,' according to what is written. As far as tutoring goes, and knowing what is a fault, and needing to take first principles and elements of the oracles of God, how would it not be thought useful? But it is slower toward the washing-off of sin, and toward being able to perfect into sanctification. And so divine Paul said to us, 'We know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those in the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and all the world may become accountable to God, because from works of Law no flesh will be justified before him; for through Law is knowledge of sins.' (Leviticus 18:5) So the Law is a shower of sin, not a bringer of boasts toward virtue. For to say, You shall not fornicate, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not swear falsely, and whatever is fitted to such things, belonged to one marking the kinds of worthlessness and putting people out of uncleanness — not bringing in a knowledge of virtue, nor making the knowledge of the unadulterated life most clear to the hearers. That one must not do the more shameful things is, I think, a dull thing to enroll among the ways of the exceptional life. I think we must, and very reasonably, only then barely bind on ourselves the vote for all the things that are praised, if, having let go of the evil and pushed it away and left it to stay down somewhere — the thing not yet rid of the reputation of worthlessness and profane abomination — we leap up onto the very boasts of virtue. before: Palladius: And what remembrance of the divine laws would become for us through fringes and a hyacinth-colored cord?
Cyril: For do you not say that the law has been spoken enigmatically to those of old and indeed also is as in shadows?
Palladius: I say so.

Cyril: An enigma then of needing to choose to think and do the things from heaven, and to remember thoroughly the laws from above—the fastening both of fringes and of the hyacinth-colored cord itself to the hand? For I think that somehow the ethereal body is imaged by the Indian stone—I mean the hyacinth—mixed with gleam and darkness, and somehow having in depth the water-like, and showing a trembling and easily-diffused look. Therefore the law has commanded economically that both from the garments themselves and indeed also from the hand the hyacinth-colored cord be hung, somehow as it were sounding under: Let a garment of mind and understanding be for you—an oracle from heaven—and let the law be awarder of right works. For the hand is a symbol of work; and the things done by us according to law are somehow altogether also unreproveable, and do not have the left-handed thing in baseness. Therefore the Pharisees were magnifying their fringes, and were widening their phylacteries—that is, the little tablets hung from the right hand; yet they were being laughed at by Christ, making the matter a starting-point of glory-loving, and not unto remembrance of the law. It is possible then even to lawless according to law, if someone should not use the law rightly. And this, I think, is what Solomon said: ‘There is a just one being destroyed in his just thing.’ (Matthew 23:5) Therefore the divine commandment must be written down unto mind and heart, and making the benefit of the matter clear the divine David said concerning every just one: ‘The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped.’ (Ecclesiastes 7:15) For it is, I think, also very clear that for whomever the divine law is present unto mind, there will also altogether be present the having been well fixed, and the lying in the firm of virtue.

before: Cyril: …the city of the living God, but somehow in a field and in a countryside, where there was no helping mystagogue, and much emptiness of those accustomed to persuade unto the better, and the deceit as in scarcity of pedagogues, let only the one who forced be in danger; for the deed is already grasping, and a suffering without help, and a necessity somehow hard to flee will turn aside the charge; or shall we say it is not superfluous to blame those upon whom things have been brought unwillingly as involuntary?
Palladius: Altogether so; for the law is holy.

Cyril: You speak well; and it makes the examination of the deeds thinner, and somehow measures the angers to the wrongs, neither releasing altogether the lesser wrong from needing to be punished, nor setting it in equality with what is beyond this, but somehow turning the motion equal-sized to the charges. For he said again: ‘And if someone should find the virgin girl who has not been betrothed, and having forced her should sleep with her, and it should be found, the human who slept with her will give to the father of the young woman fifty didrachms of silver, and she will be his wife, instead of those things for which he humbled her; he will not be able to send her away for all time.’ (Deuteronomy 22:28–29) So adultery made the one joining with a betrothed woman liable, according clearly to the modes already said. And if she should appear, he says, still unjoined, and not yet pledged to Christ through the faith, as a soul in the form of a virgin, and then someone should be caught having defiled her with words unto impiety, and having led her aside from wandering unto wandering—such a thing as heretics do, sometimes snatching those from the nations and from Jews, and persuading them to follow themselves—he will find the attempt not without penalty. Palladius: I understand what you say; for the law is double—fleshly and spiritual.

before: equity in these—is it sufficient unto being tested and tried? and having met those who twist the right things, will the one who has newly cohabited with wisdom not rather be twisted, or rather prevail and beat off those ones’ harms, not yet stepped and fixed sufficiently toward understanding?
Palladius: It seems so.
Cyril: And when someone is spurring, will the one practicing gentleness, if he is not yet somehow trained toward this, not easily go off toward anger?
Palladius: I think so.
Cyril: And an practiced wise man will fight through against wise men, and will lead out young-heartedly against those ones’ knaveries the things from rightness of reasonings?
Palladius: Truly.
Cyril: And what—will the one who has succeeded at gentleness not be hard toward angers, even if some should sometimes sharpen him toward this?
Palladius: I say so.

Cyril: Rightly therefore the law, having shaped elegantly as in a form of a woman the virtue cohabiting with the saints, ‘If someone takes a woman freshly,’ (Acts 15:28–29) it says, ‘he will not go out unto war, and no deed will be cast upon him; he will be guiltless in his house. One year he will gladden the woman whom he took.’ (Proverbs 7:4) For it does not allow the as-it-were newly fixed, and having a fresher eagerness unto the good, to be loaded with toils and persecutions, but as it were leisurely and remaining upon himself, and being warmed to be bound with the affections unto virtue. Some such thing we will find the holy apostles to have done, who to those turning from the nations, and newly called unto knowledge of God, clearly write: ‘For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to cast upon you no further burden, except that you abstain from fornication and strangled, and blood.’ (Deuteronomy 24:5) For having economically let go the more burdensome of the commandments, they were ordering to keep few and necessary things, not having been ignorant of the unenduring of hardship of those newly brought in unto the need to be pious. And indeed the God of the wholes remits such ones both anger and charges, even if they should fall into small-soulednesses, stepping through the unaccustomed road of the toils. And after this he exacts justices, and thereafter brings under the motions from anger, those no longer weak through the unaccustomed in the toils, but rather falling back unto the sweet and unsmooth, and most readily dissolving unto what is dissonant with them. In a fitting order then the Word goes forward for us, after at least the piety unto God, and the carefulness unto parents, that it is fitting that we also make the showing of fairness also unto others, he announces. For everywhere the law is seen legislating, providing for equality, and making the exact test of the just. For it has been written in Deuteronomy: ‘There will not be in your bag a great or small weight; a true just weight will be for you, and a true just measure will be for you, in order that you may become many-dayed upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you in a lot, because an abomination to the Lord your God is everyone doing these things, everyone doing an unjust thing.’ (Proverbs 16:7) And again in Leviticus: ‘In measures and weights, and with balances—just balances, and just weights, and a just chous will be for you.’ (Galatians 3:24) And with measures and weights and balances he was hurrying very well to equalize the manners of the justice, and very rightly; for a straight and justice-loving mind somehow balances and measures thoroughly the natures of the affairs, and tests the account of the equality, more finely and more exactly than someone would think those testing the coin upon a scale-pan and balance; and he measures out as it were for each of the things contemplated what is most fitting for it, neither loosing the beauty of the exact equality by the excess, nor indeed by the under-bringing toward the less allowing the sufficient as in equality to be counterfeited. Let there then be, he says, just balances and weights, and a just chous; and these would be, I think, as it were some types and clear examples, showing under for us manners through which the account of the exact equality would be searched through for us, and the knowledge of the justice will appear. For beyond just is the good—that is, the glory of the citizenship in Christ (Deuteronomy 25:13–16) (Leviticus 19:35–36).

And he convicts as destroyers and ruiners of humanity the blood-loving and falsely-named gods, who even savagely dishonor the laws of necessary affection, for the sake of what seems good to them; ‘For God created the all unto being, and the generations of the world are saving, and there is not a kingdom of Hades upon earth. Yet by envy of a devil death entered into the world.’ (Wisdom 1:14) And the divine will overturns death, and dissolves corruption; and hates that the things that are should not be; for he created the all unto being, according as it has been written. Yet those netted unto wandering by the demons’ greediness bring forward to Satan as it were seasonings, and of the most useful and sweet-smelling incense, the destruction of those come to be unto life, and the death of those created unto being. Most skillfully therefore he wished to show that the customs beside those ones are full of the last slander, and nature being wronged, and the ordinances of much-prayed-for love-of-children being trampled, very well hustling the noble and evil-hating mind of the hearers unto needing to honor and choose swiftly whatever he himself would wish and say. And these things were legislated of old unto overturning of the unholiness beside those ones. Yet he also defines death for the one wishing to persuade away the one who has been fixed, and who has received in a God-loving way the knowledge of the truth. For he said thus again: ‘And if a prophet should rise among you or a dreamer of a dream, and should give you a sign or wonder, and the sign or the wonder should come which he spoke toward you, saying: Let us go and serve other gods whom you have not known, you will not hear the words of that prophet or of that dreamer of that dream, because the Lord your God is testing you to know whether you love your God from your whole heart, and from your whole soul; behind the Lord your God you will go, and him you will fear, and his commandments you will keep, and his voice you will hear, and him you will serve, and to him you will be added. And that prophet or that dreamer of the dream will die; for he spoke to make you wander away from the Lord your God.’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14) How holy and fitting to God the law! For if indeed for murderers of bodies death must follow altogether and in every way according to laws, how would the one bringing the ruinous wandering upon a soul, and casting the better than body into pits of destruction, according to the Savior’s own voice, not reasonably be in danger? That the deceiver and buffoon must have the justice upon blood done, God judged right (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) (Deuteronomy 13:1–5) (Matthew 10:28);

before: Or does not a word carry off the equitable one and genuine lover of the life in Christ unto dogmatic rightness and unto correction of manners?
Palladius: So I say.

Cyril: Therefore two are the trumpets that gather the people upon the tent. And if they trumpet in one, he says, all the rulers leaders of sons of Israel will come toward you. For I suppose that even those more perfect in habit need consolation and encouragement, yet not so much as the multitude of the others would also need; on account of this two trumpets barely call back all the others, yet one the chosen ones; for a little suffices the wise, and if he should take a starting-point he will add what is lacking, according to the: ‘Give a wise man a starting-point, and he will be wiser; make known to a righteous man, and he will add receiving.’ (Proverbs 9:9) Then he has commanded four differences of signals to be made, so that through them those toward dawn and southwest, north and south may both break camp and set out; I think therefore that the four writings of the Gospels are signaled to us through this, through which the whole world is trained unto dogmatic and ethical science at once. And if indeed we must also invent and say something other, we will in no way shrink, making the hunt of the useful better than sleep and sweat. Of the word therefore beside us we will find four differences, through which the whole earth will set right the best and truly reputable life; one therefore and first is that through which we are accustomed to call toward recognition of truth and unto taking up of divine light those who have worshiped the creation beside the Creator, and who say unlearnedly to the wood: You are my father, and to the stone: You begot me, according to the prophet’s voice. Yet for those already having believed, the three other differences of the word would fittingly suit; since indeed the Savior also was teaching that there are three differences of life and citizenship; for he said that the seeds cast upon the good earth made fruit, one a hundred, one sixty, one thirty. Therefore there is for each of such ones the word especially fitting him; for not yet doing rightly will we benefit with equal unguarded words those divided between God and world because of being yoked under marriages according to law, and those who have taken up the all-best and ascetic life, or that fitting priesthood, but to those we will say: ‘Have you been bound to a wife? Do not seek loosing; have you been loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife;’ (Jeremiah 2:27) and as many things as it fits the married to think and do. Yet to the ascetic ones and those who have known to endure: ‘Put to death your members that are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire.’ And the: ‘The sufferings of the present time are not worthy toward the glory about to be revealed unto us.’ And to those called unto priesthood: ‘A priest’s lips will guard knowledge, and they will seek law from his mouth,’ and as many things as writing to Timothy the most wise (Colossians 3:5) (Romans 8:18) (Malachi 2:7)

before: So that even if someone of them should go upon a tomb, and throw himself upon the signs of the dead, having cast off a garment, he strips the head, and shearing it as the hair having been polluted—from which things that it was fitting to stand off and to refuse the imitation, the divine law educated us. For he said again: ‘You will not Phoebize, you will not set a baldness upon a dead one, in the midst of your eyes.’ (Leviticus 19:28) For the select of Greeks mythologize Apollo a god, whom they also name Phoebus, that is, clean and undefiled. And they say he is the same as the sun. They used to say then to Phoebize, and again to be Phoebized, according to the Greek custom, the cleansing and being cleansed, according at least to what seems to them, and the laws beside themselves. The divine oracle therefore bars us from such shameful and most unbeautiful practices. For it is not at all fitting to count the death of bodies a pollution of soul, nor indeed to think that the sight upon a dead one impresses filth upon the hearts of those seeing, nor again upon this is it fitting to strip the hair. For the matter is altogether stale and full of the ground-crawling glory. Well then the law says the ‘You will not Phoebize;’ (Isaiah 43:25) for such a cleansing will not benefit a soul, yet rather does injustice, both taking away the knowledge of the most beneficial path, and carrying away from the hunt of the advantageous. For let us look thus: Laws beside us of those ruling upon earth are, awarding and refusing the things to be done and not to those everywhere; yet no one would be able to flee the justices upon the transgressions, unless needing to be let go from the king’s mildness granting it to him. In the equal manner then, the one having disregarded the divine laws would not become clean, unless having become rich with the matter by a divine nod. For if we have transgressed laws of fire or water, and the account of the sin looks unto those, let the water wash off the writing, let the fire melt down the filth, and letting go upon authority the charges to whomever they should choose; yet if true is the one saying toward God: ‘Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done the evil before you,’ (Psalms 51:4) for one is the lawgiver and judge, instead of which having let go the lord of both punishing and letting go, they slide down into old-wives’ thoughts, distributing to fire and water the being able to free them from the charges. Away with the bad counsel, O human, approach the God alone according to nature, and you will hear him saying at once: ‘I am the one wiping out your lawlessnesses for my sake, and I will not remember.’ (Psalm 50:6 (LXX 50:6)) This is true cleansing; this is the spiritual brightness; for we have been wiped, having gained by the faith into Christ the forgiveness of the sin, yet having been made holy by the bath of regeneration, and having enriched ourselves with the divine grace, that of the divine Spirit, which also in the manner of fire consumes as some refuse the pollution that has settled into our understandings. For the God-breathed Scripture says thus justly that we have been baptized in Holy Spirit and fire.
Palladius: In a portion of idolatry then will we somehow reckon also the wandering upon this (Titus 3:5) (Matthew 3:11) (Luke 3:16) (Psalm 51:4 (LXX 50:6))?

before: Neither oath, nor faith, nor prophets’ Sayings having tested, you cast me out of land unjudged. Theseus toward this said: This tablet not having received a lot Accuses you faithfully; yet the birds going above the head, I say farewell much. And indeed God’s voice would become trustworthy, and the faith better than the writing in a tablet, if somehow it is also not unlikely for us to speak false; yet to sin nothing is God’s, and the true is most especially dear. Yet Theseus somehow knew altogether that the birds going above the head are nothing completely. Therefore one must not yet ascribe the knowledge of the things about to be to demons, yet rather we will distribute it to God as exceptional. And trickery will be hereafter—the birds’ prophecies—and a clear proof of an unsafe understanding—the faith upon this. And somewhere also the law itself says: ‘You will not use bird-omens,’ (James 5:14–15) knowing the matter abominable, and most especially abominated beside the God ruling all.
Palladius: Thus these things seem to me myself also to hold.

Cyril: And since again this secret and old-wives’ whispering would also be a portion and manner of sorcery. Therefore also the divine Moses clarified the laws from above for us, always joining the stumblings, and somehow as it were setting the charm in brotherhood and same-nature with the drug-working. ‘For there will not be,’ he was saying, ‘in you one prophesying a prophecy, using bird-omens and omen-taking, a drug-worker, a charmer, a wonder-watcher, and a ventriloquist, and one asking the dead.’ (Deuteronomy 18:10–11) Yet the charm is sick with the all-shameful altogether, and with lying very much in evil, yet somehow some have been fluttered unto this, saying that—Lord Sabaoth they name while charming over the sick, the caretakers of such things. In this way then they also hurry to confirm that the practice would not be shameful hereafter. Yet they seem to be carried off by a cold and inactive reasoning unto deceit and mind-harm; therefore this very thing is that the matter is most hard to bear. For we cry out the ‘Lord Sabaoth’ to the God of the wholes, wishing to doxologize; yet to no other of the things that are do we grant to have such a calling. For one and alone is the Lord of the powers. Yet they easily cast aside the thus supernatural and most glorious surname—or then doxology—to whichever of the demons playing together with them they should choose, and to the actors of their wonder-working they gift the glory most fitting for God and him alone, both flattering and being flattered, and distributing the excess of such terrible impiety of the running-together upon whatever they should choose unto a counter-payment. For always God-fighting and most glory-loving is the band of the demons. Therefore we must not be carried off together with those ones’ bad counsels, yet rather stand off as farthest, and not pay attention to wicked healers or wonder-workers—the demons—asking as some wage of the playthings unto us the blasphe

before: Cyril went on: That is, either one who has ended by a law of nature, or one forced out by the murderers. For you, he said, have temples and precincts, bolts and gates, inside which, having perhaps run in, it will be possible to sacrifice purely, as you yourselves think according to yourselves; but we, sacrificing of necessity in the middle of a city, in crossroads and in fields, are defiled by the sights of the dead. For there is wholly nothing to keep it off by bounds. And the word of the history would have for us the persuasive in the customs of the Egyptians, and what was said by Moses, who was wise in all things, would be rightly said, even if it should be understood spiritually. For we must sacrifice as in a wilderness, and complete a holy feast to God, setting out from the Egyptians', and also refuse the sight of death. For with a leisured mind, and one that has come to stand far from being darkened in a worldly way, and setting the eye free from the things that carry it down into deadness and corruption, we shall sacrifice purely to the God who rules all. And dead works would be the things of the flesh. And worldly darkening is the muddying from evil and vain distractions, defiling the clean and clear ether of the mind. That it is fitting for those who wish to worship purely to be separated from these, the word of the history also persuades us.
Palladius said: And this at least is not unclear; so complete for me what follows.

Cyril: So then a hard-to-bear and sharp longing for the ancient freedom ran in, I think, upon those from Israel; and already having turned aside toward this, they provoked terribly to angers the one who binds them in the yokes of slavery. And saying that the desires upon such things are a work of leisure, he commands that the sweat upon the works be stretched tight for them, the accustomed quota being demanded without delay, and the distribution of the straw being cut off from them contrary to custom; for he said that 'You are idle, you are idlers; because of this you say, Let us go and sacrifice to our God. Now then go and work; for the straw shall not be given, and you yourselves shall give the quota of the brickmaking. So the scribes of the sons of Israel saw themselves in evils, saying: You shall not fall short of the brickmaking, the due for the day. And they met Moses and Aaron coming to meet them, as they were going out from Pharaoh, and they said to them: May God look upon you, and judge, because you have made our smell abominable before Pharaoh and before his servants, to give a sword into his hands to kill us.' (Exodus 5:8–9) (Exodus 5:17–21) For, my friend, do you not say it is exact, that whenever someone should choose to loose himself from the yoke of the devil's greed, and to take up instead the bright and free boast of the worship toward God, and to be still and to know the true Master, according to what is sung in the Psalms: 'Be still and know that I am the Lord God,' (Psalm 46:10) he will accuse us of the leisure and will upon this as an unholy thing.

before: Cyril: …he does not allow to be in danger, for the works of night and darkness are punished, but the things as in light thereafter no longer. And God has justified release from the ancient charges, and from those in ignorance and darkness. And indeed let it also be said to those who have arrived from sin unto the intelligible light, ‘You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.’ (Ephesians 5:8) Thus the Lord has also justified the divine Paul, who was formerly a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent man; for beyond measure he persecuted the Church of God and was laying it waste.
Palladius: You have spoken most excellently.

Cyril: And if he should not be able, he says, five calves instead of one, and four sheep instead of one, let him be sold instead of the theft. You see how the law clearly writes down the slavish dishonor of those who have continuous and unwashed-out sin, and who are not even able, so to speak, to beat off the charges with ransom, both through weakness of resolve not enduring to sweat unto repentance, and through the labors unto this to propitiate God? But some disobeyed Christ’s Gospel, and not having accepted the redemption from the sin, bear it again as a burden, having hung it upon their own heads through weakness of mind, and softness of understanding and unmanliness of soul. These are carried about by every evil wind, and being most violently pushed together unto every form of uncleanness they make as much eagerness as possible unto the base things. And a sign of eagerness is the wing, which he also says is of a hoopoe, and this is a form of a small bird, always running round the most foul-smelling of the marshes, and gathering from mire and uncleanness unto food. As many therefore as spend their own eagernesses unto pollution, these would altogether reasonably be said to have the hoopoe’s wings. And they themselves are womanlike, and made soft, and thereafter conformed to the sin tyrannizing against them. For in the manner those under him and with him have become conformed to Christ through sanctification, so also those loaded with the lawlessness, and having chosen to live together with unclean baseness, are conformed and like-formed to it. Thus also the law was proclaiming beforehand clearly the season of our Savior’s slaughter, which we say he has endured on behalf of the world’s life: ‘For on the tenth,’ (Exodus 12:3) it says, ‘of the first month, let them take for themselves a sheep according to houses; according to a number,’ (Matthew 20:1–7) it says, ‘of soul they will collect, and it will be kept until the fourteenth of this month, and all the multitude of the sons of Israel will slaughter it toward evening.’ (Exodus 12:3-6) Do you hear how having been taken from a tenth, the victim was kept for those of old unto a fourteenth, in order that you may understand the fifth season, according to which having become human he underwent the death on our behalf, the moon already waning, which has also been set unto beginnings of the night? And the matter is a type of a mystery, and seems to signify thinly the devil’s greediness’s path backward, and a sinking as it were the little-by-little unto the strengthless and altogether weak. And somehow he holds a type of moon. For he also rules

before: Palladius said: I would reasonably ask, then, what the delay of the sanctification according to faith was — why you say the sign is in the older place and the thing that surpasses it in the second.

Cyril: Did we not just say that it was the work of an admirable and unspeakable skill, that the Law which condemns should leap up in time before the faith that justifies? Or does not the light shine in the darkness? And is not power perfected in weakness, according to what is written?
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: So the Law came in besides, so that the trespass might increase. For where there is no Law, there is no transgression either. And how would anyone see the forgiveness of transgression and of the ease toward it, if the Law had not first condemned us? That what I say is true, and that the argument on this is not some faded or ugly thing, Paul will help, saying, 'So the Law was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom it has been promised, ordained through angels.' (Galatians 3:19) And being very wise, he tries to cut off in advance the inventions and questions that will sometimes be found by some. For it was likely that some would blame the delay of the righteousness in faith, and say that the coming-in of the Law in between became a setting-aside of that ancient promise. That is why he says, 'Is the Law then against the promises of God (Galatians 3:21)? Let it not be. For if a Law had been given that was able to make alive, righteousness would truly have been in Law. But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Before the faith came, we were guarded under Law, being shut up into the faith about to be revealed to us. So the Law became our tutor unto Christ, so that we might be justified from faith. But when the faith has come we are no longer under a tutor, for you are all sons of God through the faith in Christ Jesus.' (Galatians 3:25)

And he makes the question white-clear, as it were, by adding, 'This I say: a covenant previously ratified by God, the Law that came after four hundred and thirty years does not annul, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance is from Law, it is no longer from promise. But God has granted it to Abraham through a promise.' (Galatians 3:18) So the Law, having shut us up into sin, tutored us unto Christ, for the end of Law and prophets is Christ. That is why he also said to the peoples of the Jews who had not believed him, 'If you believed Moses, you would believe me. For he wrote about me.' (John 5:46) We are justified, then, not from works of Law, but rather by the faith in Christ. 'For as many as are from works of Law are under a curse. For it is written, Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them. But from the curse of the Law Christ bought all, having become' (Galatians 3:10) (Deuteronomy 27:26) (Galatians 3:13)

For through us it was written, that the one plowing ought to plow upon hope, and the one threshing upon hope of partaking.’ Calves therefore, according to the image of the first—that is, of Christ—are also the blessed disciples. And Christ is a threshing calf also otherwise; for through him is the cleansing and the putting-away of superfluous things—I mean distractions and the fleshly thoughts according to the world, which are also food of flame, just as also the chaff. And the altar having been raised, upon which also a peace-offering and the whole-burnt-offering, what grieves has been loosed; for the Lord listened to the earth, and the breaking was held together. For Christ having priested himself for us, death was abolished, and corruption was overturned, the God who is able in all things somehow already holding ready the ear for the prayers of all; for ‘While you are still speaking,’ (1 Corinthians 9:9–10) he says, ‘I will say: What is it?’ (Isaiah 65:24) And the altar’s being small at the beginnings, and saying it was added to it later, makes clear the progress of the Gospel that will come to be according to times, and of the holy Churches the being contracted at the beginnings, and breadth as it were also in what follows. For the altars are as it were always being widened, Churches always somehow being added to the first ones with others, and the peoples being stretched unto an unmeasured multitude, who have been redeemed through the sacrifice in Christ, having him as sacred minister and the holy victim, and fragrant thoroughly cleansing, and as an altar worth admiring, and as in a form of the threshing-floor the Church’s master.

Palladius: In what manner do you say?

Cyril: The law was a practice unto justice and as it were some pre-entry of the Gospel manly-deeds. For it has been written: ‘A beginning of a good way is to do the just things.’ (1 Corinthians 13:5–8) For the law pedagogues unto Christ, and of the life understood in him it would not have a falsified glory, if it should be understood spiritually. And it stands unto justice, yet carries off still beyond this—the Gospel lesson. And manners of justice—first, honor and loving, the one unto the one and by nature God; and neighboring as it were and after that at once the one unto brothers and same-raced, the reverence unto parents having been set beforehand. In a fitting order then the Word goes forward for us, after at least the piety unto God, and the carefulness unto parents, that it is fitting that we also make the showing of fairness also unto others, he announces. Cyril: I will speak. Dwelling long times with Egyptians, those from Israel, and having slipped into every kind of sin, and delighting in the local luxuries, Moses did not ignore that they will be slow and very hard to move toward good order; yet he was wisely taking that the toil of the works will push them toward obedience unwillingly, if they should see him working wonders. Cyril: You have spoken most rightly. For having let go the needing to worship God who is according to nature, they turned childishly toward useless random-worship; pouring shame and laughter upon their own head, and having chosen a self-called falling-away from the help from above. And indeed God said: ‘As a thief’s shame when he is caught, so will the sons of Israel themselves be shamed, and their kings, and their rulers, and their priests, and their prophets; to the wood they said, You are my father, and to the stone: You begot me. And they turned backs upon me, and not their faces; and in the time of their evils they will say: Rise and save us. And where are your gods, whom you made for yourself? If they will rise and save you in the time of your ill-treatment? because according to the number of your cities were your gods, Judah, and according to the number of Jerusalem’s ways they were sacrificing to Baal. Why do you speak toward me? All you have lawlessly acted unto me, says the Lord.’
Palladius: Terrible truly is the matter, friend.

Cyril: Yet someone sometimes of those finishing among us, not yet very much fixed, yet having practiced a plastered and bastard love unto Christ, and such as putting around himself as it were a fleece the seeming to be God-loving, will be a bitter and unholy beast, both a monkey and facing-both-ways, so as at home and by night—I mean the having-escaped-notice—to cling to the demons’ worships, and somehow to think reasonably that he himself also can run past God, and out-reason the mind of the unspeakable nature. And one would show even very without-toil that the one for whom these things are present to think has chosen the more shameful things of the Greeks’ silliness. For to the wise beside Greeks it seemed to hold rightly that the sun, being created and begotten—the great light-bearer, and made upon this very thing from beside God—sees all and hears all; for they thought that what has been taken along in a God’s rank must be rich with the dignities of the divine nature. And a dignity of the highest nature is to know and look down upon the all. Yet those ones in these things; and to us God was calling of old: ‘I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God from far; will anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23) For nothing would escape the one who is truly God by nature. And let blessed David mystagogue saying: ‘Understand already, senseless ones among the people, and fools, sometime be thoughtful; the one who planted the ear, will he not hear? and the one who shaped eyes, will he not understand?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24) Some were saying, I think, from ununderstanding: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’ (Psalm 94:7) Or is it not altogether silly to say that the supplier of knowledge neither knows, nor to think that the one giving the matter to those come to be from beside him does not hear (Psalm 94:7)?

before: Cyril: …completion according to flesh they were practicing, having been transferred unto the worship of the law; for this very reason they were also making the formation of Christ in themselves incomplete, somehow aborting the good lying in themselves as in a womb. So the perfect in knowledge and the unmixed unto faith will house the formation of the Savior in the souls of all of us, and this in us will be as somehow a divine sowing. Whenever then some should be scandalized as from the word-fight of certain ones; and then the soul that has suffered this should abort the faith and knowledge lying as in travails and treasured within unto mind—if it should be, he says, not yet formed, that is, if still incomplete and less beautiful, the cause of the scandal will altogether and in every way endure a penalty, which the bridegroom of this one should lay on, he says—that is, Christ; and he will give with dignity, that is, let him also confess grace, not having undergone the penalty unto complete destruction. And if the intelligible conception of the soul should be formed, he says—that is, if there should be knowledge and faith of Christ wearing formation—he will be subject to the accounts concerning the last things, as already also a murderer. For death of soul is the putting-off of the blameless faith, and the loss of knowledge that holds rightly. Therefore he says that needing to share unholy teachings, and whatever words a man would make, having become devilish prey, and somehow food of the herd of demons, is a pollution; and he forbids again, saying as in a riddle, ‘And flesh taken by beasts you will not eat; throw it to the dog.’ (Exodus 22:31) For it is custom of the divine Scripture to name as dog the shameless and unclean human. And every word somehow foul and stinking would be fitting for such a one, I think, and composed from Beelzebul himself, as of a wild beast having eaten down the soul that fell under him and serves unto this; ‘For no one says, Anathema Jesus, except in Beelzebul.’ (1 Corinthians 12:3) And for holy ones to come into participation of thoughts and words so shameful or adulterated is altogether unfitting. ‘For there is no communion of light toward darkness.’ (1 Corinthians 12:3)
Palladius: Truly.
